claims.text: The target materials are nanoparticles containing at least five metals in nearly equal atomic ratios and initially forming a single-phase solid solution.
Electronegativity and atomic-mass differences among constituent elements are primary drivers of local chemical fluctuations.
Local chemical fluctuations produce heterogeneous lattice distortion and strain fields.
Selecting elements with contrasting properties can tailor local chemical fluctuations and associated strain.
Nonuniform local chemical environments arise from differences in constituent-element properties.
Local strain fields inhibit rapid elemental diffusion and phase segregation.
The strain fields elevate the energy barrier for atomic rearrangement.
Elevated atomic-rearrangement barriers preserve the single-phase structure and prevent chemical segregation during extended high-temperature operation.
Local strain stabilizes high-entropy nanoparticles as single-phase solid solutions throughout 473–1923 K.
Nanoparticles engineered for stronger local chemical fluctuations will exhibit less phase segregation than nanoparticles with more uniform elemental properties.
Nanoparticles engineered for stronger local chemical fluctuations will retain consistent catalytic surface properties.
Nanoparticles engineered for stronger local chemical fluctuations will maintain thermoelectric performance across 473–1923 K.
Nanoparticles with diminished local fluctuations will be more susceptible to phase instability and elemental clustering at elevated temperatures.
At lower temperatures, the baseline single-phase nanoparticles exhibit minimal elemental diffusion and phase separation.
The proposed stabilization is expected under inert or minimally oxidizing conditions between 473 and 1923 K.
Strongly oxidizing environments, dominant external chemical reactions, or temperatures outside the tested range may override the local-strain stabilization effect.
Electronegativity, mass, and atomic radius may contribute by quantitatively different amounts to stabilization.

contradictions.description: The comparison is said to use identical overall compositions while one set includes elements with substantially different electronegativities and masses and the control uses elements with more similar properties. Changing elemental identities or their balance changes the overall composition, so the proposed control cannot simultaneously satisfy both requirements unless only atomic arrangements—not constituent selection—are varied.
